parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *-ъka, compare Romanian -ică.

parole.significato: weeping willow, a willow with very pendulous twigs, of cultivars or hybrids of Salix babylonica
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *orkyta (“broom, kind of willow”). Compare Serbo-Croatian rakita and Bulgarian ракита (rakita).

Based on an unattested adjective derived from Proto-Slavic *bogatъ (“rich”) or going back to the otherwise unregistered Proto-Slavic *bogatьje (“richness”). According to Topalli, the final -i is a native suffix. Compare related adjective i/e begatë.

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian baština (“inheritance”) from Bulgarian баща (bašta, “father, governor, patriarch”) which is derived from Proto-Slavic *batę (“older brother, daddy”). A rather late borrowing, considering the preserved unstressed vowel, and lack of rhotaci
Derived from Proto-Slavic *bělъka ("white animal"), from *bělъ ("white").
Derived from Proto-Slavic *bělica (“white object”), from Proto-Slavic *bělъ (“white”).
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *bělъ (“white”) + -ush. Compare Serbo-Croatian bel and Macedonian бел (bel).
From Proto-Slavic *bělъ (“white”) + -shtë. Compare Serbo-Croatian bel and Macedonian бел (bel).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *bělъ (“white”) + -zgë. Compare Serbo-Croatian bel and Macedonian бел (bel).

From a South Slavic language, ultimately Proto-Slavic *božurъ (“peony”), from *bogъ (“god”). Compare Serbo-Croatian божур, Bulgarian божур (božur). Also borrowed into Romanian bujor and Hungarian bazsarózsa.
Ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *čerenь.

From a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic дꙑхати (dyxati, “to breathe, to blow”) and archaic Serbo-Croatian dihati (“to breathe”) (modern disati); ultimately from Proto-Slavic *dyxati (“to breathe”), a derivative of *dyxъ (“whiff”).

From dialectal i udobë (“easy”), from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic оудобь (udobĭ, “easy”) and Serbo-Croatian udoban (“comfortable”); ultimately from Proto-Slavic *dobъ (“good, well, nice”). Orel describes it as derived from an earlier dobë, whence dobi (“benefit”), borrowed i

Either from *torbar, based on torbë (“shepherd's bag; knapsack”), or from a phonetic transformation *dobëri, from Proto-Slavic *dobro (“property”). Compare Old Armenian տուար (tuar), Proto-Germanic *tībrą (whence Old English tifer, Old High German zebar (“sacrificial animal”)).
A -th suffixed formation from an unattested *drokë, possibly from Proto-Slavic *drokь (“genista”), which, however, is not attested in South Slavic.

Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *galъ; compare Serbo-Croatian gȁo (“black, dark”), Bulgarian гал (gal, “jackdaw”). While the meaning ‘black sheep’ is attested in Serbo-Croatian гаља (galja), the meaning ‘jackdaw’ is only attested in East Slavic: Russian галя (galja).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, derived from Proto-Slavic *globa (“fine”). Compare Serbo-Croatian globa (“fine, penalty”) and Bulgarian глоба (globa, “fine”).
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *gorьnica.

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic грабити (grabiti), Serbo-Croatian grabiti (“to grab, to sieze”) and Bulgarian грабя (grabja, “to rob, to plunder”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *grabiti (“to grab, to sieze”).

parole.significato: a large mythological serpent with two heads
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *grabǫšnęš (“a mythological snake that drinks from cattle udders”). Compare Serbo-Croatian grabonos. Topalli suggests that the final -ofç is derived from an optative verbal suffix.

parole.significato: manger, place where livestock eat fodder
parole.testo: From a South Slavic language, especially eastern dialects, compare Old Church Slavonic граждь (graždĭ, “manger”), Bulgarian гражд (gražd, “barn”); ultimately from Proto-Slavic *gorďь (“fence”), related to Proto-Slavic *gordъ (“fortification, town”).
From Proto-Slavic *goršь, derived from *gorxъ. The West Slavic development of *-or- may point towards a derivation from an extinct dialect.
From Proto-Slavic *glъtiti. Compare Latin gluttiō.
Derived from Proto-Slavic *glъtiti.
Possibly a verbal formation of unattested *gërd/gërdë, derived from Proto-Slavic *gъrdъ (“ugly”). Compare Serbo-Croatian grditi ("to disfigure") and Serbo-Croatian grd ("ugly").
Disputed: * According to Orel, from Proto-Slavic *kъrxati (“to cough, expectorate”), cognate to Serbo-Croatian kȑhati. * According to Çabej, an onomatopoeia or cognate of Albanian grahmë.
From Proto-Slavic *grьkъ, from Latin graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós). Compare Serbo-Croatian Grk, Bulgarian грък (grăk). Ultimately a doublet of grek.
Either borrowed from an unattested Proto-Slavic *gъrdlačь, or directly derived from *gъrdlo (“throat”).
A relatively early borrowing from Proto-Slavic *gromada. See also Romanian grămadă.
From Proto-Slavic *grьkyni. Compare Serbo-Croatian Gȑkinja, Czech Řekyně. Ultimately a doublet of greke.
Ultimately from a Proto-Slavic *vorbьľь (“sparrow”), unattested in most South Slavic dialects, where only *vorbьcь is found.
Most probably from Proto-Slavic *gъrnъ. Compare Belarusian го́ран (hóran).
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *xukati.
From Proto-Slavic *jьskra, cf. Serbo-Croatian iskra, Bulgarian искра (iskra), among others.

parole.significato: a mythological figure imagined as a revenant that picks fights during the night, especially with drunks
parole.testo: According to Orel borrowed from Proto-Slavic *judъ ~ *juda, while Çabej and Lambertz link it with the figure of Judas.
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *jùgъ (“south (wind)”) (cf. South Slavic Bulgarian and Serbo-Croatian jug (“south”)).
Singularized plural of *karavalë, derived from Proto-Slavic *korvajь (“round bread”) through a South Slavic language; compare Serbo-Croatian kravaj.

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic казньць (kaznĭcĭ) ("chamberlain, person in charge of the treasury") a court title of state employees in medieval Bosnia and Serbia. Ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *kaznь, which was inherited into Serbo-Croatian kazna ("punishme
Derived from Proto-Slavic *tъkačь, compare Bulgarian тъкач (tăkač).
An early Slavic loanword, from Proto-Slavic *kočubъ ~ *kočuba ("crest, tuft"). Topalli suggests a derivation from cub (“short-tailed”).

Orel suggests a derivation from Proto-Slavic *kočura (“hummock”), which is otherwise unattested in South Slavic and poses semantic problems. Topalli argued an internal formation from çurrel (“thin stream of water”).
Derived from Proto-Slavic *kobь through a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian kob (“fate, destiny, omen”) and Bulgarian коба (koba).
From Proto-Slavic *kopati (“to dig, hollow out”). Compare Bulgarian копач (kopač, “sapper”), копа́я (kopája), Serbo-Croatian kopati. Also note Romanian copac, Aromanian cupaci.
From a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian kopar and Bulgarian копър (kopăr). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *koprъ.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian koriti ("to scold, reprimand, criticize") or Old Church Slavonic корити (koriti) ("to jeer at"), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *koriti.

From a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic квасъ (kvasŭ, “sour dough, sour drink”), archaic Serbo-Croatian квас (“yeast”), Slovene kvas (“yeast”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kvasъ (“leaven, fermented drink”).

A later borrowing from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian kòsa (“scythe”) and Bulgarian коса (kosa, “scythe”). Ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *kosa (“scythe”). Non-Slavic cognates include Greek κόσα (kósa), Romanian coasă, and Hungarian kasza.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *korľь (“king”).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian ključ (“key”), Old Church Slavonic ключь (ključĭ), and Bulgarian ключ (ključ). Ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *kľučь (“key”).

Suffixed form of an unattested noun *lakëm, from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic лакомъ (lakomŭ, “hungry”), Serbo-Croatian лаком (“greedy, covetous”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *olkomъ (“greedy”).

Most likely a formation after lëndë (“timber”), similarly to the connection of vis with vend. Alternatively, Orel suggests a borrowing from Proto-Slavic *lěsъ (“forest, woods”), whence Serbo-Croatian lȇs /ле̑с, Bulgarian лес (les), although in this case one would expect the auslaut to have undergone

Variant of dialectal (Visokë) llo (“moisture, dampness”), from Proto-Slavic *lojь (“suet, tallow”); cf. Bulgarian лой (loj), Serbo-Croatian lȏj. Doublet of lojë. Svane/Ylli prefer a different loan from Bulgarian ло́ква (lókva, “puddle; (dial.) flood plain”).
Uncertain. Per Orel, borrowed from Proto-Slavic *loska, but unattested in South Slavic languages except for Old Slovene lusk (“tick”).
Alternative variant of macë (“cat”), ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *maca, likely an onomatopoeic expression.
Derived from macë (“cat”) (macë from Proto-Slavic *maca).
From Proto-Slavic *maca. See Albanian mace (“cat”) for more.
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *maxnǫti (“to shake, move”), *maxati. Compare Serbo-Croatian máhnuti (“to wave”), máhati.
From a South Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *němьcь (“foreigner”), from *němъ (“mute”). Compare Serbo-Croatian Nemac (“a German”), Macedonian Немец (Nemec), Bulgarian немец (nemec).
Derived from Proto-Slavic *moldika (“young tall tree”) through a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian mladikа and Bulgarian младика (mladika).
Derived from Proto-Slavic *močalъ through a South Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian močar.
According to Orel, borrowed from Proto-Slavic *mušica (see Serbo-Croatian mušica).
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *mъzga (“rainy weather”).

parole.significato: plants like great mullein or heather, often used to make brooms
parole.testo: According to Lafe, most likely a borrowing from Proto-Slavic *metъla, whence also the Balkan Romance *metula. Çabej also proposed to derive this word from a Venetian *nètola (an otherwise unattested derivative of netar ‘to clean’). This, however, would not account for the Balkan Romance and Slavic f
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *oborъ (compare Bulgarian обо́р (obór), Serbo-Croatian òbor).
From a South Slavic language, ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *agnьcь (“lamb”), compare Old Church Slavonic агньць (agnĭcĭ, “lamb”), Bulgarian а́гнец (ágnec).

parole.significato: meadow by a forest or grove, which is used for grazing
parole.testo: From dialectal Montenegrin ograđa, compare standard Serbo-Croatian ograda (“fence, enclosure”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *o(b)gordъ, a derivative of *gordъ (“settlement, enclosure”).

parole.significato: inula, elecampane (Inula spp., especially Inula helenium)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *omanъ.
According to Orel, sense 1 is an early borrowing from Proto-Slavic *pǫdarь. For sense 2 and sense 3, derived from pendë (“plough animals yoked together”) + -ar.
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *poľakъ.
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *polata (“palace, porch”). The shepharding term was borrowed to Romanian poiată.
A relatively recent denominative formation, based on prisk(ë), borrowed from Proto-Slavic *pryskъ (whence South Slavic *prъskati).

Together with proseqe (“chips, chippings (from a pruned tree)”), a Slavic loanword from Proto-Slavic *prosěkъ (“kind of axe; opening, cutting (in a forest)”). Compare Bulgarian просек (prosek), Serbo-Croatian prosijek. The meaning presented in Albanian is not attested in South Slavic; a development

parole.significato: a short message or note written on a piece of paper and sent to somebody
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *posъlъ, from *sъlъ (“messenger”). Compare Proto-Slavic *sъlati (“to send”). Dizdari suggests a borrowing from Turkish pusula.

An early loanword from a South Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *rędъ (“row, line”) with a preserved nasal. Compare Old Church Slavonic рѧдъ (rędŭ, “line, order”), Serbo-Croatian red (“row”), Bulgarian ред (red, “row”), and West Slavic descendant Polish rząd (“row”).
From Proto-Slavic *sanь, compare Serbo-Croatian saoni.

parole.significato: poor farmers who take turns using a team of oxen to which each contributes one ox
parole.testo: Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *sębrъ (“fellow”).
From Proto-Slavic *sěra (“sulphur”). Cognate to Serbo-Croatian sjera, Bulgarian сяра (sjara).
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *sapъ (“glanders”). Compare Bulgarian сап (sap).
Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *(š)četъka.
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *skopiti.
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *sokolъ (see Serbo-Croatian sokol, Bulgarian соко́л (sokól)).
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *slota. The variant shqotë preserves the original substantiation of Proto-Slavic *sl- > Proto-Albanian *skl-.
From Proto-Slavic *stьrvъ (see Serbo-Croatian strvina).

Orel derives it from Proto-Slavic *stъrviti (“to bait, to lure, to train”); compare Bulgarian стръвя (străvja) < стръв (străv, “bait”). Topalli instead considers it a prefixed form of vit (“year”), initially used for livestock that take up certain tasks once they reach one year of age.

Orel derives it from Proto-Slavic *stъrviti (“to bait, to lure, to train”); compare Bulgarian стръвя (străvja) < стръв (străv, “bait”). Topalli instead considers it a prefixed form of vit (“year”), initially used for livestock that take up certain tasks once they reach one year of age.

From a regionally attested sund (“supervision, seizure, capture, reign, protection”). Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic сѫдъ (sǫdŭ) ("trial, court") and Serbo-Croatian suditi; ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sǫdi (“judge”). Doublet of sodit.
From a South Slavic language, derived from Proto-Slavic *tękъ (“appetite”). Compare Serbo-Croatian tek (“appetite”).
From Proto-Slavic *termъ (see Serbo-Croatian trem).
An early borrowing from a South Slavic language (owing to the preservation of the nasal), ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *trǫtiti. Compare Serbo-Croatian truditi.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian trup, Bulgarian труп (trup). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *trupъ.

parole.significato: tang, blunt side, part of a blade or axe where the wooden handle in put
parole.testo: Possibly from dialectal Bulgarian тун (tun, “false; wrong”), implying “the wrong part of the blade”, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *tuňь (“futile”).
Based on an unattested *tërpis (“to suffer, ensure, bear”), from Proto-Slavic *tьrpěti. Cognate to Serbo-Croatian tŕpeti, Bulgarian търпя (tărpja).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian ugar (“fallow land”) and Macedonian угар (ugar, “fallow land”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ugorъ (“fallow ground”).

parole.significato: fish trap, net (mainly for catching eels)
parole.testo: From plural form of Proto-Slavic *volkъ.

Used mostly in its mediopassive form venitem. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *vędnǫti. Compare Serbo-Croatian venuti, Bulgarian вена (vena). Regarding divergent verbal suffix, compare Slovene veniti and Upper Sorbian wjadnyć.

From an adverb vesht, a locative of vesh (“ear”) according to Gazulli. Alternatively derived from Proto-Slavic *věštъ, compare Serbo-Croatian vešt, where connection with vesh would be through folk etymology.

A loanword from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic влага (vlaga, “moisture”), Serbo-Croatian влага (“moisture”); ultimately from Proto-Slavic *volga (“moisture”). Although a connection with lag (“moisten”) has been proposed (Miklošič, Meyer), they are likely unrelated (yet, contami

From a noun vobek/vobeg, a singularized plural of *vobog, from a South Slavic language; compare Old Church Slavonic оубогъ (ubogŭ, “wretched, poor”), Serbo-Croatian убог (“poor, miserable”), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ubogъ (“poor”).
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *vьlkolakъ (“werewolf, vampire”).

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Old Church Slavonic забѣль (zabělĭ) ("enclosed forest"), and modern Serbo-Croatian zabijeliti ("to whiten, to mark a tree by cutting its bark"), used in Dušan's Code as ("mark a tree by cutting its bark to show forbidden entrance"). Ultimately from Prot
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *žegъ. Compare Serbo-Croatian žega (“sun-heat”).

parole.significato: scorched residue stuck to the bottom of a cooking pot
parole.testo: From South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *žigъ.
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *zidъ. Compare Romanian zid, Aromanian zid.
Borrowed from Proto-Slavic *suša (“drought”), with an irregular z-. Compare Serbo-Croatian suša, Bulgarian суша (suša).
From a South Slavic language, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *ščetina (“bristle”). Compare Serbo-Croatian četina, Macedonian четина (četina).

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *čudo (“miracle, wonder”). Compare Serbo-Croatian čudo (“miracle, wonder”) and Bulgarian чудо (čudo, “miracle”); compare also Romanian ciudă (“fury, grudge, envy”), Hungarian csoda (“miracle, wonder”). Initially rendered as

parole.significato: a rugged hill without vegetation, barren ground
parole.testo: From the same root of bukël, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoHu (“to grow, swell”). Compare Old High German buhil (“hill”). See also bukur. Alternatively from Serbo-Croatian bok (“side, flank”), ultimately from Proto-Slavic *bokъ (“side”). However, Svane casts doubt over the Slavic source, owing to its

Either an inherited term, or a Slavic borrowing. Çabej deems it as inherited from Proto-Indo-European, listing Proto-Slavic *dolto (“chisel”) and Latin dolō (“to hew”) as cognates, and linking it internally with deltinë (“clay”). Çabej's arguments are based on the lack of archaic borrowings from Sla

From Proto-Albanian *krau, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₂u, *ḱrh₂eu (“limb”). Close to Latin crūs. Alternatively from archaic krahi, definite krai (Buzuku), from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *krajь (“end; rim, edge; region”) (compare Serbo-Croatian krȃj, Bulgarian край (kraj)). Similar sense dev
Borrowed from Latin clupea, via dissimilation and methatesis. Alternatively from Proto-Slavic *kъlbь.

parole.significato: field (in a forest); flat ground, area, lawn
parole.testo: From Proto-Albanian *lēga, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ- (“to put down, lie down”). Compare Old Frisian lōch, Dutch oorlog (“war”), Middle High German urlage (“fate, battle”), Old English log (“place”), Old Norse løgi (“tranquillity”), Greek λόχος (lóchos, “confinement”), Tocharian A lake, Tochari

Borrowed from a South Slavic language, ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic *lędina (“untilled land”); compare Serbo-Croatian lèdina, Bulgarian леди́на (ledína). Alternatively connected to lëndë, although seemingly unlikely, or perhaps directly from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ-.
Possibly from Proto-Slavic *marěna (“madder”), which however cannot be found in South Slavic. Alternatively from Italian amarena, regionally marena (“sour cherry”).

Probably from lengthened and diathematic e-grade form Proto-Albanian *mel-i-t-ja, from Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“to hesitate; bad, wrong, false”). Compare Greek μόλις (mólis, “with difficulty”), Old Irish mall (“be late”). Alternatively from Proto-Slavic *mъdьliti.

Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately either from Proto-Slavic *pàdati (“fall”) whence Serbo-Croatian nà-padati /на̀-падати (“to attack”) or from Proto-Slavic *pǫditi (“to chase”) whence Macedonian пади (padi, “to chase out”).

A term with multiple plausible etymologies. Either from Latin rāpum (“turnip”), Ancient Greek ῥάπυς (rhápus, “turnip”), or Proto-Slavic *rěpa (“turnip, beet”), or natively from Proto-Indo-European *(s)rā́ps. First attested as rrap, producing the contemporary form through plural metaphony and the Arb

parole.significato: female gown (made of wool, covering the shoulders and the chest)
parole.testo: Either from Proto-Germanic *sarkiz (“shirt, armour, hauberk”), via Gothic or from Proto-Slavic *sorka (“shirt”). Schuhard and Meyer claim a borrowing from either Latin serica or Latin sarica.
